title: Customers Who Have Placed at Least One Order
description:
Find all customers who have placed at least one order using an EXISTS subquery.

**Table: customers** — `id`, `name`, `email`

**Table: orders** — `id`, `customer_id`, `amount`

Output columns: `name`, `email`. Order by `name`.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id INT, name VARCHAR, email VARCHAR); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Alice','alice@example.com'),(2,'Bob','bob@example.com'),(3,'Carol','carol@example.com'),(4,'Dave','dave@example.com'),(5,'Eve','eve@example.com'),(6,'Frank','frank@example.com'); CREATE TABLE orders (id INT, customer_id INT, amount DECIMAL(10,2)); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,120.00),(2,1,85.00),(3,2,200.00),(4,3,50.00),(5,4,310.00),(6,4,95.00),(7,5,175.00);
solution_sql: SELECT name, email FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY name

test_cases.description: 6 customers; Frank (id=6) has no orders, so 5 customers are returned

hints: EXISTS returns TRUE as soon as the subquery finds any matching row — it does not need to count or return data.
The subquery correlates to the outer query through o.customer_id = c.id, checking each customer individually.
explanation: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id) returns TRUE for customers 1-5 who all have at least one order. Customer 6 (Frank) has no matching rows in orders so EXISTS returns FALSE and Frank is excluded. EXISTS is more efficient than IN with large datasets because it short-circuits on the first match.
